sections.Business:
The company builds high-performance chips and software for a wide range of computing needs, with a particular focus on artificial intelligence. Its products include processors, graphics chips, networking components, and programmable chips used in data centers, personal computers, gaming consoles, and embedded systems in industries like automotive, healthcare, and industrial equipment. The company was the first to put a dedicated AI processing unit alongside an x86 processor in a mainstream PC chip, and it offers a full software stack to help developers build and run AI applications across different platforms and hardware.

A major strategic priority has been expanding its data center business, driven by strong demand for AI accelerator chips from large cloud computing customers. The company launched new generations of its Instinct GPU series and its 5th Gen EPYC server processors in 2025, and previewed a full rack-scale AI platform called "Helios" combining its CPUs, GPUs, and networking products. It also struck a significant deal with OpenAI to deploy 6 gigawatts of its GPUs, with the first gigawatt powered by its Instinct MI450 series — a partnership intended to demonstrate its ability to deliver complete hardware and software solutions at scale.

To strengthen its position, the company made several acquisitions during the year. It bought ZT Systems in March 2025 to gain design capabilities for AI infrastructure, though it later sold ZT's manufacturing operations to Sanmina Corporation in October 2025. Other acquisitions targeted software improvements, high-speed networking, and AI inference capabilities. The company reorganized its reporting structure, merging its Client and Gaming segments into one, leaving it with three reported business segments: Data Center, Client and Gaming, and Embedded.
sections.Risk Factors:
The business faces intense competition in fast-moving markets where success depends on delivering high-performing, energy-efficient, and competitively priced products on time. Major rivals like Intel and Nvidia use their dominant market positions, financial strength, and proprietary software ecosystems to undercut pricing, lock in customers, and limit alternatives. In September 2025, Nvidia announced a partnership and investment in Intel aimed at new data center and client platform products, which could increase pricing pressure and block other opportunities. Competitors pursuing alternative chip architectures, such as Arm, also pose a growing threat across consumer, commercial, and data center markets, and some customers are developing their own chips internally to handle AI workloads.

The semiconductor industry goes through sharp boom-and-bust cycles, and the business has suffered heavy losses during past downturns due to falling prices, supply and demand imbalances, and weakening end-user demand. Global economic uncertainty has historically caused consumers and businesses to delay purchases, hurting product demand. The rise of AI is adding new pressure on the industry to design and deliver chips quickly enough to meet surging demand for computing power and AI infrastructure. Growth also depends on emerging global markets, and if demand there falls short of expectations, sales could decline significantly.

Demand for products is tied closely to the health of the broader industries they serve, meaning a slowdown in any key end market can directly hurt results. The business also faces risks from relying heavily on outside manufacturers, which creates vulnerabilities around production capacity, yields, and access to essential materials and equipment. Cybersecurity threats, IT disruptions, and data breaches could damage operations and expose sensitive intellectual property. On top of this, export controls, tariffs, tax changes, ongoing litigation, and evolving regulations around AI and environmental standards all add further uncertainty to the business outlook.

sections.Cybersecurity:
The company has built a cybersecurity risk management program designed to protect its critical systems and information. The program is guided by the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and AI Risk Management Framework, though this doesn't mean the company meets any specific technical standards — these are simply used as references. Key elements of the program include regular risk assessments, an internal security team, third-party security testing, employee training, an incident response plan, and a vendor risk management process that includes security assessments based on each vendor's risk profile. Cybersecurity risk is also folded into the company's broader enterprise risk management efforts.

As of the time of filing, no known cybersecurity threats or past incidents have materially affected the company's operations, business strategy, financial results, or financial condition. However, the company acknowledges that ongoing cybersecurity threats exist and could, if they materialized, cause meaningful harm to the business.

On the governance side, the Board has assigned oversight of cybersecurity risks to its Audit and Finance Committee, which receives quarterly updates from management and is briefed on any significant incidents as they arise. The full Board gets at least one cybersecurity briefing per year. Day-to-day responsibility for the program sits with the Chief Information Security Officer, who reports to the Chief Information Officer and has over 20 years of experience across areas including security operations, cloud security, and identity and access management.
sections.Properties:
As of December 27, 2025, the company occupies approximately 6.8 million square feet of space worldwide, used for research and development, engineering, administration, and warehousing. Of that total, about 5.4 million square feet is leased and 1.4 million square feet is owned. The main headquarters is in Santa Clara, California, with major operations in cities including Austin, Texas; San Jose, California; Shanghai, China; Markham, Ontario; Longmont, Colorado; Dublin, Ireland; Singapore; and Bengaluru and Hyderabad, India.

In addition to these core locations, the company maintains regional sales offices in commercial centers close to customers, primarily across the United States, Europe, Asia, and Latin America. The company does not expect any significant problems renewing leases or finding replacement facilities if needed.

The company considers its current facilities to be appropriate and sufficient for its present needs, and believes that the available capacity is either already being used or is planned to be put to use in the near future.

sections.Market for Registrant\u2019s Common Equi:
The company's common stock trades on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under the ticker "AMD." As of January 30, 2026, there were 5,094 registered holders, and the stock's closing price that day was $236.73 per share.

The company has a board-approved stock repurchase program allowing it to buy back up to $14 billion of its own shares, funded through cash from operations. The program has no expiration date and can be paused or cancelled at any time. No shares were repurchased during the final three months of fiscal 2025, and as of December 27, 2025, $9.4 billion of that authorization remained unused.

Separately, when employees' equity awards vest or are exercised, the company withholds some shares to cover the employees' tax obligations. These withheld shares count as repurchases in an accounting sense but are not part of the formal $14 billion buyback program. During fiscal year 2025, approximately 3.8 million shares were withheld this way at an average price of $164.86 per share.
sections.[Reserved]:
Starting from a base value of $100 in December 2020, the company's stock grew to $159 by the end of 2021, then dropped sharply to $71 in 2022. It recovered strongly to $161 in 2023, dipped slightly to $136 in 2024, and then climbed to $234 by December 2025, representing a total gain of 134% over the five-year period.

By comparison, the S&P 500 Index showed steadier and more modest growth over the same period, rising from $100 to $201 by December 2025. The S&P 500 Semiconductors Index dramatically outperformed both, surging from $100 to $547 over the same five years, driven by a particularly strong run from 2023 onward.

While the company's stock ultimately outpaced the broad S&P 500 by the end of the period, it lagged well behind the semiconductor sector index, which more than quintupled in value. The company's path was also considerably more volatile, with a steep mid-period decline before its eventual recovery and growth.
sections.Management\u2019s Discussion and Analysi:
Revenue grew sharply in 2025, rising 34% to $34.6 billion from $25.8 billion the prior year. The biggest drivers were the Data Center segment, which brought in $16.6 billion (up 32%), fueled by demand for server processors and AI GPUs, and the combined Client and Gaming segment, which generated $14.6 billion (up 51%) on strong sales of Ryzen processors, game console chips, and Radeon GPUs. The Embedded segment was the one weak spot, slipping 3% to $3.5 billion. Gross margin edged up to 50% from 49%, though that improvement was partially offset by roughly $440 million in net inventory and related charges tied to U.S. export restrictions on certain AI GPU products sold into China. Cash and short-term investments ended the year at $10.6 billion, up from $5.1 billion, while total debt rose to $3.3 billion from $1.8 billion. The company also returned $1.3 billion to shareholders by buying back 12.4 million shares, with $9.4 billion still available under the repurchase program.

Two major deals shaped the year. In March 2025, the company acquired ZT Systems for $3.2 billion in cash plus 8.3 million shares of stock, keeping its design operations and intellectual property. It then sold ZT's manufacturing business to Sanmina Corporation in October for $2.4 billion in cash plus Sanmina stock, with up to $450 million more in potential payments depending on certain conditions being met. Separately, a large product agreement was signed with OpenAI to deploy 6 gigawatts of AI GPUs, and as part of that deal, OpenAI received a warrant to buy up to 160 million shares of common stock at essentially no cost — but only if specific purchase and stock price milestones are hit. As of year-end, none of those conditions had been met, so the warrant had no financial impact.

A significant risk during the year came from U.S. government export controls. New restrictions on selling certain AI GPU products to China led to approximately $800 million in inventory charges in the second quarter. After securing some licenses to ship to select Chinese customers, the company reversed about $360 million of those charges in the fourth quarter once shipments resumed. An additional complication remains unresolved: U.S. officials have indicated they expect to receive 15% of revenue from licensed sales into China, but no formal regulation requiring that payment has been published yet, leaving the ultimate financial obligation unclear.
sections.Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosure:
The company faces interest rate risk primarily through its investment portfolio, which as of December 27, 2025 consisted of fixed income instruments, time deposits, and commercial paper. The portfolio is managed conservatively, with investments limited to high credit quality issuers and no single issuer receiving too large a share. A hypothetical shift of 50 basis points in interest rates would have affected the fair value of the cash equivalent and investment portfolio by approximately $25 million. All long-term debt carries fixed interest rates, so changes in market rates have minimal impact on reported interest expense. To guard against default risk, all debt securities in the portfolio were A-rated by at least one rating agency as of that date, and the company only holds securities with active resale markets to maintain liquidity.

The company also holds long-term investments in both publicly traded and privately held companies. As of December 27, 2025, investments in publicly traded companies were valued at $198 million, up from $0 at the end of the prior year. Non-marketable equity securities and other instruments — which include early-stage, privately held companies whose technologies may never reach maturity — grew from $468 million to $1.3 billion over the same period. These investments carry meaningful risk, as the underlying technologies are often still in development and could result in a total loss.

Because the company operates internationally, it incurs costs and holds assets in foreign currencies even though most product sales are priced in U.S. dollars. To manage this exposure, the company uses foreign currency forward contracts and does not use these instruments for speculation. As of December 27, 2025, those contracts had a total notional value of $3.4 billion, up from $2.8 billion a year earlier, covering currencies including the Indian Rupee, Canadian Dollar, and Chinese Renminbi. The net fair value of the forward contracts shifted from a $66 million loss at the end of 2024 to a $12 million gain as of December 27, 2025, with all contracts set to mature within 24 months.
sections.Financial Statements and Supplementary D:
Revenue grew sharply over the three-year period, rising from $22,680 million in 2023 to $25,785 million in 2024 and then to $34,639 million in 2025. Net income followed a similar upward path, climbing from $854 million in 2023 to $1,641 million in 2024 and reaching $4,335 million in 2025. Diluted earnings per share rose from $0.53 to $1.00 and then to $2.65 over the same period. Operating income also improved significantly, going from $401 million in 2023 to $3,694 million in 2025, reflecting better leverage on higher sales even as spending on research and development and marketing increased considerably.

The balance sheet shows total assets of $76,926 million at the end of 2025, up from $69,226 million a year earlier. A large portion of those assets — $25,126 million in goodwill and $16,705 million in acquisition-related intangibles — reflects past acquisitions. Cash and short-term investments together totaled $10,552 million at year-end 2025, compared to $5,132 million at the end of 2024. Inventories grew to $7,920 million from $5,734 million, and total stockholders' equity increased to $62,999 million. The company also repurchased $1,316 million of its own stock during 2025 and spent $625 million covering employee tax obligations tied to equity compensation.

Cash generated from operations reached $7,709 million in 2025, a substantial jump from $3,041 million in 2024, driven by higher earnings and contributions from discontinued operations. The company used $5,533 million in investing activities, including $974 million in property and equipment purchases, $1,760 million in acquisitions, and $5,470 million in short-term investment purchases, partially offset by proceeds from a divestiture and maturing investments. On the financing side, the company raised $2,441 million through new debt while repaying $950 million. Management notes that preparing these financial statements requires judgment calls in areas such as inventory valuation, goodwill assessment, and income taxes, and actual results could differ materially from the estimates used.
sections.Changes in and Disagreements with Accoun:
There were no disagreements with the company's accountants on any accounting or financial disclosure matters during the period covered by this filing. The company maintains internal controls designed to ensure that required information is properly recorded, summarized, and reported on time, and that key decision-makers like the CEO and CFO receive that information when they need it. Management acknowledges that no control system can guarantee perfect results, but aims for reasonable assurance.

As of December 27, 2025, the CEO and CFO completed an evaluation of whether the company's disclosure controls were working effectively. These evaluations are done every quarter to monitor performance and make adjustments as needed. Based on that review, both executives concluded that the disclosure controls and procedures were effective at the reasonable assurance level as of that date.

The company also maintains internal controls over financial reporting, which are processes overseen by the CEO, CFO, Board of Directors, and other staff. These controls are meant to ensure that financial records accurately reflect the company's transactions, that money is only spent with proper authorization, and that any unauthorized use of company assets is detected quickly. The company acknowledges that these controls cannot provide absolute certainty, but are designed to provide reasonable assurance that financial statements are reliable and prepared in accordance with standard U.S. accounting rules.
sections.Controls and Procedures:
Management evaluated the company's disclosure controls and procedures as of December 27, 2025, and concluded that they were effective at a reasonable assurance level. This evaluation was carried out with the involvement of the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer, and the same type of review is performed every quarter to monitor whether controls are working properly and to make adjustments as needed. The goal is to ensure that information required in regulatory filings is captured, processed, and reported accurately and on time.

The company also maintains internal controls over financial reporting, which are designed to give reasonable assurance that financial statements are prepared accurately and that company assets are properly managed. These controls are meant to ensure transactions are recorded correctly, that spending is only made with proper authorization, and that any unauthorized use or mishandling of assets is detected or prevented before it can meaningfully affect the financial statements.

However, management acknowledges that no internal control system can offer absolute guarantees. These controls rely on people, which means they are vulnerable to human error, poor judgment, or even deliberate circumvention through collusion or management override. Because of these built-in limitations, there remains some risk that errors or misstatements could go undetected. The company recognizes this and aims to build safeguards into its processes to reduce that risk, even though it cannot be fully eliminated.
sections.Other Information:
Management reviewed its internal controls over financial reporting using an established framework and concluded that those controls were effective as of December 27, 2025. This conclusion was independently verified by Ernst & Young LLP, which issued its own attestation report confirming the findings. No changes were made to internal controls during the most recently completed fiscal quarter that had, or were likely to have, a meaningful impact on how those controls function.

During the quarter ended December 27, 2025, one executive made a notable update to their stock trading arrangements. On November 14, 2025, the Executive Vice President and Chief Technology Officer, Mark Papermaster, adopted a formal stock trading plan under Rule 10b5-1, which provides a legal framework allowing company insiders to sell shares at pre-scheduled times without running into insider trading concerns. Under this plan, up to 124,936 shares of common stock may be sold, and the plan is set to run until November 16, 2026, unless ended earlier according to its terms.

No other director or officer activity related to such trading plans was reported for the period, and the section on foreign jurisdiction inspection disclosures was listed as not applicable. Taken together, this portion of the filing confirms that financial reporting controls are functioning properly, that an independent auditor agrees with that assessment, and that a senior technology executive has put a structured plan in place to manage future stock sales.
